questions.text: Why use a block-diagonal attention mask when packing patch sequences from different images into one sequence?

options.A: To let every patch attend to every image in the batch.
options.B: To reduce every image to the same number of patch tokens.
options.C: To replace all patch-position information with image labels.
options.D: To restrict each patch to attending within its own image.

questions.explanation: Concatenation places images in one sequence; the mask prevents cross-image attention while allowing attention within each image.

questions.text: Your frozen vision encoder accepts only 336×336 inputs, but you need fine detail from a large document image. Which strategy fits this constraint?

options.A: Resize the full document to 336×336 and discard all local detail.
options.B: Use AnyRes tiles plus a global thumbnail, encoding each at 336×336.
options.C: Send the full native-resolution image to the fixed-size encoder unchanged.
options.D: Use a packing mask to make every patch contain more pixels.

questions.explanation: AnyRes applies the fixed-size encoder to separate tiles and a global thumbnail, retaining more local detail at a higher visual token cost.

questions.text: pack_batch receives image token lengths [2, 3]. It accumulates offsets from [0] and sums n*n for mask_nonzero. What are cu_seqlens and mask_nonzero?
questions.explanation: Cumulative offsets are 0, 2, 2+3=5. The two within-image blocks contain 2²+3²=13 allowed cells, compared with 25 dense cells.
